title: 163 Characterizing performance, forage intake, and feed efficiency in beef heifers fed a grass hay diet using residual feed intake and residual average daily gain
content:
Abstract
The objective of this study was to characterize performance (ADG) and forage intake (DMI) in beef replacement heifers classified for forage efficiency using residual feed intake (RFI) and residual average daily gain (rADG). Fifty-five fall-born yearling Angus heifers [initial body weight (BW) = 321 ± 24.8 kg] were divided into two dry lot pens based on initial body weight at the Oklahoma State University Range Cow Research Center. Dry lot pens equipped with individual intake monitoring feed intake units (C-Lock Inc., Rapid City, SD) fitted with hay baskets. The study consisted of a 21-d adaptation followed by 71-d of data collection. Salt/mineral/vitamin supplement and hay (12% CP and 56% TDN) were provided on an ad libitum basis. The multiple regression equation to predict DMI (R2 = 0.51) included mid-test body weight0.75 (MBW), and ADG. The multiple regression equation to predict ADG (R2 = 0.24) included MBW and DMI. There was a moderate negative correlation between RFI and rADG (r = -.468). Heifers were classified by k-means clustering into three categories of forage efficiency based on RFI and rADG. Data was analyzed using the General Linear Model Procedure of SAS to determine the effect of RFI or rADG on the performance metrics of heifers. Heifers classified as efficient consumed 20% less forage (P < 0.01) compared to heifers classified as inefficient with no differences in initial BW, final BW, or ADG (P = 0.80). Heifers classified as efficient according to rADG gained 0.27 kg more (P <.001) per day compared to those classified as inefficient with no difference (P>0.60), in BW or DMI. Relative performance and forage intake differences among efficiency classifications in heifers fed a strict forage diet were similar to results reported in the literature using energy-dense, processed diets.
